newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania bows to pressure from West on elections.
newsitem.headline: Albania bows to pressure from West on elections.

text.p: Albania's conservative President Sali Berisha has bowed to pressure from Europe and the United States by giving opposition parties a bigger role in the running of nationwide local elections in October.
Berisha met leaders of 14 political parties, including the main opposition Socialists, at a round-table discussion in Tirana late on Wednesday to outline his concessions.

"Election commissions at every level...should have a vice chairman from the opposition in all their presidencies who has the right to sign and vote on all the decisions it takes," a statement from the president's office said.

The make-up of electoral commissions ahead of a general election last May was a main grievance among opposition parties, who complained that representation on the bodies was slanted towards Berisha's rightist Democratic Party.
Nearly all opposition parties boycotted the election, claiming the poll was rigged, and refuse to take up the few parliamentary seats they won. The Democrats won 122 seats in the 140-member assembly.

Many opposition concerns were given added weight when foreign observers from the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe issued a report criticising the poll as failing to meet all the criteria for democratic elections.
During the all-party talks on Wednesday night, Berisha also agreed to amend a controversial law which bars former communist officials from public office and the judiciary until 2001.
The legislation, also criticised by some Western governments, effectively removed many of Berisha's leftist rivals from standing as candidates in the general election.
In the local polls scheduled for October 20, the law will only apply to candidates seeking the post of mayor but not to those standing for other posts on local councils.

Political leaders also agreed that state-run television, the only channel broadcast nationwide in Albania, should give equal time to the government and the opposition. During the general election campaign, the television came under attack for bias towards the Democrats.

The crucial changes were agreed a week after a delegation from the Council of Europe told Berisha that Albania could be suspended from the body unless the government and opposition made moves to settle their differences.

The European Union has cautioned Tirana that it will be closely watching the local elections to gauge Albania's commitment to democracy. The U.S. State Department last month urged the Democrats to involve the opposition in the local polls and advised them to consider holding a fresh general election at the earliest opportunity.
The concessions appear to have won enough support from the Socialists, heirs to the former communist party, who had threated to stay away from the local elections.
"The Socialist Party expressed its readiness to take part in local elections to counter the propaganda that tried to push it towards a boycott," said senior Socialist Et'hem Ruka.
